description: Project Eclipse is built by a team of three friends. Reshma leads the team and builds the app, turning our ideas into something playable. Nitish handles research and storytelling, shaping the space science and the world of the game. Shanmukh puts together our presentations and keeps us prepared. We each own a part, give each other blunt feedback, and fix things instead of arguing over them.
summary:
Project Eclipse is a browser game where you design, fly and manage a whole space mission, and feel every trade-off instead of reading about it.

The story: on a sunless planet, 24 orbital stations called Lanterns light the cities. Lantern 17 is failing and a giant ice fragment is coming. You are the engineer sent to find out why. You build a ship inside a 100-credit budget (or take a ready-made beginner package), choose a route, fly it yourself under real orbital gravity, dodge ice and dock. Then you walk the station, gather proof, run a test, make one hard decision and report to the network.

Every choice gains something and costs something, and the costs come from real physics (the rocket equation, Hohmann transfers, communication time, shield limits) built on published NASA figures. Every number is tagged real, game value or fiction. There are eight endings, and a debrief explains why you won or lost and lets you replay with one change.

It answers the challenge's call for integrated trade-offs, random events, limited resources, mission reports and teaching the "why". A verified engine (137 automated tests) powers it, and it runs in any browser with no install.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Project Eclipse is an interactive space mission design game that runs in any browser. You are the engineer sent to find out why Lantern 17, one of 24 orbital stations that light a sunless planet, is failing. You build a spacecraft inside a 100-credit budget (or take one of five ready-made beginner packages), choose a route, fly it yourself under real orbital gravity, dodge a tracked ice fragment and dock. Then you walk the station, inspect six zones, gather six clues, run a controlled test, make one hard decision and report your proof to the network.

HOW IT WORKS

One game engine checks every click and writes a plain-English ledger line, so any mission can be replayed exactly. The costs come from real physics: the ideal rocket equation (a heavier shield means less delta-v), Hohmann and fast transfers, communication time (file size divided by link speed) and shield ballistic limits. Every number is tagged real, game value or fiction, so players can see where the science ends and the story begins.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students usually memorise mission trade-offs from a textbook. Here they feel them: after one mission a player can explain why every kilogram, hour and watt costs something, and why speed, evidence and time pull against each other. A debrief explains why the mission succeeded or failed, shows the real hardware behind each part the player used, and lets them replay with one change. Plain-language part cards, beginner packages and a guided mode make it usable with no space background.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

It is a story-led mission with eight different endings, where proof, timing and choices all matter. It includes a first-person station walk with a thermal visor and a physically modelled test beam.

TOOLS

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Three.js and custom WebGL shaders, Vitest (137 automated tests that re-derive every physics number and play whole missions). Hosted on Vercel, code on GitHub. AI: Claude Code helped write the code and ElevenLabs made the voice lines.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Mass, power, budget, communications, time and orbit, plus accessibility: it works on phones, with a keyboard alone, and with reduced motion.
